question: Move the AED at P.S. 197 John B. Russwurm into a 24/7 outdoor cabinet on the building's street wall.

evidence.text: P.S. 197 John B. Russwurm (School, ZIP 10037) has a registered AED at "outside main office; Basement, Outside Gym".
Its hours come from: School building assumed open 7 AM to 6 PM on school days, September to June. Move the school-hours control to test other closing times.
Under that assumption it is reachable 55 of 168 hours in a school-year week, and 0 hours in a summer week if it is a school.
In 2025, an expected 1.28 cardiac-arrest 911 calls a year came from inside its two-minute walking area at hours when every AED in reach was shut (rank 4 of 100 NYC schools).
Within 400 m there are 3 other registered AED locations; 0 of them are open 24/7 by their published hours.
Citywide, a time-blind map puts 4.6% of call-weighted area within a two-minute walk of an AED; at the hour calls actually came in, 1.4% was within reach of one confirmed open.
Published research: a bystander shock with a public AED was associated with survival to discharge of 66.5% versus 43.0% without (Pollack et al., Circulation 2018, observed shockable public arrests).
Overture Maps lists FDNY EMS Station 16, a fire station normally staffed around the clock, 103 m away: a possible alternative host for a 24/7 AED.
Unknown to this data: cabinet cost, vandalism risk, whether the school already allows after-hours access, and the actual location of each 2025 call inside the ZIP (only ZIP-level data is public).

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: Moving this AED to a 24/7 outdoor cabinet addresses a real gap in coverage. The school's current location is unreachable during 113 hours each week when school is closed [E3], and in 2025 an estimated 1.28 cardiac arrests occurred in the surrounding area during times when no nearby AED was accessible [E4]. Research shows bystander use of public AEDs is associated with survival rates of 66.5 percent versus 43.0 percent without [E7]. The three other AEDs within walking distance are not open 24/7 [E5], making this move a practical way to improve emergency response capacity in this neighborhood.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The advocate identifies a real coverage gap, but the proposal's urgency and feasibility remain unclear. Yes, 1.28 cardiac arrests annually occurred when nearby AEDs were inaccessible [E4], but that's a small number spread across a large area—we don't know if those calls were actually near P.S. 197 or elsewhere in the ZIP [E9]. The survival benefit from public AEDs is substantial [E7], yet citywide only 1.4 percent of call-weighted area reaches an open AED at actual call times [E6], suggesting the problem is systemic, not specific to this school. Before moving this AED, we should explore the fire station 103 meters away [E8], which is already staffed 24/7 and might host a cabinet more reliably. We also lack critical information: cabinet cost, vandalism risk, and whether the school permits after-hours access [E9]. Those unknowns could make this expensive or impractical compared to alternatives.

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: The skeptic is right that the fire station alternative deserves exploration [E8], but it doesn't eliminate the case for moving this AED. The station is 103 meters away—still outside the two-minute walking radius for many residents in the coverage gap. More importantly, we know this AED exists and is currently trapped behind school hours [E3]. Moving it to outdoor access costs nothing in terms of acquisition and directly converts an existing asset into round-the-clock coverage. The skeptic's call for more information [E9] is reasonable, but shouldn't delay action on a known, addressable problem while we study alternatives that may never materialize.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The advocate is right that moving an existing AED is faster than building new infrastructure, but speed shouldn't override due diligence on a permanent decision. The fire station alternative at 103 meters [E8] may actually serve the gap better: it's already staffed 24/7, eliminating vandalism and maintenance risks that could leave the school's cabinet inoperable when needed most [E9]. We don't know if the school will permit reliable after-hours access or what cabinet costs are [E9]. Before converting this asset, we should confirm whether FDNY can host a cabinet there. The citywide problem is systemic—only 1.4 percent of call-weighted area reaches an open AED when calls actually occur [E6]—so one school's move alone won't solve neighborhood cardiac arrest mortality. Explore the fire station first.

verdict.summary: Real coverage gap exists (1.28 arrests/year unreachable [E4]), but unknowns about cost, vandalism, school access [E9], and a viable alternative 103m away [E8] warrant investigation before permanent relocation.
verdict.strongestFor: Current AED unreachable 113 weekly hours [E3]; 66.5% survival with public AED vs 43.0% without [E7].
verdict.strongestAgainst: Unknown call locations within ZIP [E9]; fire station alternative 103m away already 24/7 staffed [E8]; critical unknowns: cost, vandalism, access permission [E9].
verdict.nextStep: Contact FDNY Station 16 to assess feasibility and timeline for hosting a 24/7 AED cabinet before relocating school's unit.
